title: Motorsport Strategy Lab: cross-championship race-strategy models and a retrospective audit of 1,280 real pit-stop decisions
description:
Race-strategy models are typically fitted and validated within one championship, often within one race. This work applies one protocol across four championships and seven car classes — Formula 1, WEC, IMSA and ELMS — and asks two questions the existing literature rarely does: does a fitted degradation slope predict a season it has never seen, and does a time-optimal planner stop where teams stopped.

Transfer is mostly not measurable from public timing. Of 51 circuit-classes measured by leaving one season out, only 5 reach a within-stint R² of 0.2. Inside a stint the fuel burned nearly cancels the tyre’s wear, so even a slope stable by construction could not reach 0.2 at 16 of 22 Formula 1 circuits and 43 of 50 endurance circuit-classes. Measured directly as a variance component, the slope moves between races by a median of about a third of its mean. The raw difference between GT3 and prototype classes (+0.164, 95% CI [+0.059, +0.312], permutation p = 0.0011) falls to +0.035 [−0.005, +0.085] when classes are paired within the events that run both, so no difference between car types is claimed.

Held to the team’s strategy, the planner agrees with teams, and the agreement comes from the horizon. Run to the flag, a single-next-stop planner stopped later than teams on 80% of Formula 1 decisions, by a median of 12 laps on those, because it answered a different question from a team that had already planned a second stop. Replaying 1,280 real first pit stops with each team’s next stop held fixed, it lands a median of +3 laps [+2, +4] from the Formula 1 team out of sample, and a rule that only balances tyre age before that stop does as well in every class.

The stops carry what the fit misses. Read as an implied wear ratio, teams’ stint lengths follow compound hardness in both directions of change (0.73 to a harder compound, 1.74 to a softer one), on the side hardness predicts for 79% of decisions against 48% for the fitted slopes.

A note on the endurance planner: across 205 race-seasons the class-level correlation between median pit loss and the tyre-limited share is −0.982 on six class points, and 150 race-seasons above a 22.5 s pit loss contain no tyre-limited race; the regime is close to an identity of the planner and is reported as a description.

Endurance lap timing derives from the DuckDB hf://datasets/tobil/imsa, curated by the IMSA Data Scraper Project from IMSA WeatherTech official results and released under the MIT License; THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md in the repository records that and carries the upstream notice. The CC BY-NC-SA terms below apply to this project's own code, models and derived output, not to that upstream material.

What underwrites it. Every quantity is measured from published timing or absent; nothing is imputed. Standard errors are cluster-robust throughout. Two estimators built for this work were validated on synthetic races and then withdrawn when they failed on real fields, and those withdrawals are described rather than omitted. Every artifact derived from committed data is regenerated in continuous integration, which fails on any difference between the working tree and the repository. The manuscript contains no numbers of its own: every quantity is a macro generated from the committed artifacts.
